title: Finding V max and K M in a patient

segs.text: Module eight, objective three. Finding V max and K M in a patient. C p is the plasma concentration, the drug level. V max, the fastest rate at which the enzymes can eliminate the drug, is a rate: an amount or concentration per unit of time. K M is the drug level at which the elimination rate is half of V max. Since C p and K M are both concentrations, a level is low or high only when compared with K M. She said, We can compare because they've got the same units. V max and K M are constant in one patient but differ between patients. Her slide example gives K M ten milligrams per liter and V max twelve milligrams per kilogram per day.

card.m: C<sub>p</sub>: the plasma concentration, mg/L
V<sub>max</sub>: the fastest elimination rate, a rate, e.g. mg/kg/day
K<sub>M</sub>: the concentration at which rate = ½ V<sub>max</sub>, mg/L
K<sub>M</sub> on the C<sub>p</sub> axis; V<sub>max</sub> on the rate axis
compare C<sub>p</sub> with K<sub>M</sub> (both mg/L)
constants in one patient, different between patients
her example: K<sub>M</sub> 10 mg/L, V<sub>max</sub> 12 mg/kg/day

segs.text: Why does the order of elimination, first or zero, change with the level? The rate is the amount removed per unit of time; depends on concentration means this amount changes with the level, even if the fraction removed does not. Well below K M, the rate is a small part of V max, so the enzymes have spare capacity, and twice the level gives about twice the rate: first order. Well above K M, the enzymes are saturated: more drug raises the rate only a little, so it stays near V max: zero order. Low and high always mean relative to K M, a concentration, never relative to V max, which is a rate. The half life is nearly constant well below K M and lengthens as the level rises.

card.m: rate = amount removed per time; depends on concentration = this amount changes with C<sub>p</sub>
C<sub>p</sub> ≪ K<sub>M</sub>: twice C<sub>p</sub>, about twice the rate → first order
e.g. (K<sub>M</sub> 10, V<sub>max</sub> 12) C<sub>p</sub> 0.5 → 1 mg/L: rate 0.57 → 1.09 mg/kg/day (× 1.9); 0.57 is about 5% of V<sub>max</sub>
C<sub>p</sub> ≫ K<sub>M</sub>: saturated, rate ≈ V<sub>max</sub> → zero order
e.g. C<sub>p</sub> 100 → 200 mg/L (beyond the graph): rate 10.9 → 11.4 mg/kg/day (× 1.05)
low or high: compared with KM (mg/L). Vmax is a rate (mg/kg/day), never compared with a level.
C<sub>p</sub> ≪ K<sub>M</sub>: the amount removed per time follows C<sub>p</sub>; the fraction and t<sub>½</sub> stay nearly constant. t<sub>½</sub> lengthens as C<sub>p</sub> rises.

segs.text: The elimination rate equals V max times C p, divided by K M plus C p. C p on the top raises the rate, and C p on the bottom, added to K M, limits how far it can rise. When C p is much smaller than K M, adding it hardly changes the bottom, which stays about K M, so the rate is about V max over K M times C p: a constant times the level, which is why twice the level gave about twice the rate. When C p is much larger than K M, the bottom is about C p, the C p on the top and the bottom cancel, and the rate is about V max whatever the level: zero order.

card.m: rate = {{frac:V<sub>max</sub> C<sub>p</sub>|K<sub>M</sub> + C<sub>p</sub>}}
C<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>M</sub>: rate = {{frac:V<sub>max</sub> K<sub>M</sub>|2 K<sub>M</sub>}} = ½ V<sub>max</sub>
C<sub>p</sub> ≪ K<sub>M</sub>: K<sub>M</sub> + C<sub>p</sub> ≈ K<sub>M</sub> (e.g. 10 + 0.5 = 10.5 ≈ 10)
rate ≈ {{frac:V<sub>max</sub>|K<sub>M</sub>}} C<sub>p</sub>: a constant × C<sub>p</sub>, like first order
C<sub>p</sub> ≫ K<sub>M</sub>: K<sub>M</sub> + C<sub>p</sub> ≈ C<sub>p</sub>, so rate ≈ V<sub>max</sub>, a constant, like zero order

segs.text: At steady state the drug going in each day equals the drug eliminated each day, so the daily dose rate R equals the elimination rate, and the level is C s s, the steady state concentration. This gives the dose rate equation: R equals V max times C s s, over K M plus C s s. Well below K M, C s s rises nearly in proportion to R. As R nears V max, the elimination rate is close to V max, so C s s has to climb steeply, and a small change in dose gives a large change in concentration. For a drug like this, steady state takes two to three weeks, not three to five half lives.

card.m: steady state: rate in = rate out, so R = elimination rate
R = {{frac:V<sub>max</sub> C<sub>ss</sub>|K<sub>M</sub> + C<sub>ss</sub>}}
turned around: C<sub>ss</sub> = {{frac:R K<sub>M</sub>|V<sub>max</sub> − R}}
R near V<sub>max</sub>: a small rise in R, a large rise in C<sub>ss</sub>
steady state: 2 to 3 weeks

segs.text: Her slide example shows this in a seventy two kilogram patient. A pair is one dose rate and the steady state level it produced. On six milligrams per kilogram per day the level was ten milligrams per liter. A linear drug keeps the level in proportion to the dose, so eight would have given about thirteen. Instead, eight milligrams per kilogram per day gave twenty: one third more dose doubled the level, because elimination was saturating.

card.m: pair 1: R<sub>1</sub> = 6 mg/kg/day → C<sub>1</sub> = 10 mg/L
linear: {{frac:10 × 8|6}} = 13.3 mg/L
pair 2: R<sub>2</sub> = 8 mg/kg/day → C<sub>2</sub> = 20 mg/L

segs.text: One pair is not enough, because the dose rate equation has two unknowns, V max and K M. Two pairs from the same patient share one V max and one K M. Solving each pair's equation for V max and setting the two equal removes V max and leaves K M, which is why K M comes first. This is the direct method. K M equals the difference R two minus R one, divided by the difference between R one over C one and R two over C two.

card.m: two pairs, one patient: one V<sub>max</sub>, one K<sub>M</sub>
V<sub>max</sub> = {{frac:R<sub>1</sub>|C<sub>1</sub>}}K<sub>M</sub> + R<sub>1</sub> = {{frac:R<sub>2</sub>|C<sub>2</sub>}}K<sub>M</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>
K<sub>M</sub> = {{frac:R<sub>2</sub> − R<sub>1</sub>|(R<sub>1</sub>/C<sub>1</sub>) − (R<sub>2</sub>/C<sub>2</sub>)}}

segs.text: Pair one is the lower dose rate. Each ratio on the bottom, a dose rate divided by its own level, is the patient's clearance per kilogram at that level, V max over K M plus C s s, from objective two. Clearance falls as the level rises, so the lower dose has the larger ratio. The top takes the higher dose rate minus the lower, and the bottom takes the lower dose's ratio minus the higher dose's, so both differences are positive and so is K M. The units leave a concentration. For her pairs the ratios are zero point six and zero point four, and K M is ten milligrams per liter.

card.m: {{frac:R|C<sub>ss</sub>}} = {{frac:V<sub>max</sub>|K<sub>M</sub> + C<sub>ss</sub>}} = Cl<sub>T</sub>, clearance (per kg here)
top 8 − 6 > 0, bottom 0.6 − 0.4 > 0
{{frac:mg/kg/day|(mg/kg/day) per (mg/L)}} = mg/L

segs.text: With K M known, V max comes from the dose rate equation rearranged: V max equals R times the sum K M plus C s s, all divided by C s s, with one pair's R and that same pair's level. From the second pair, eight times thirty, over twenty, is twelve milligrams per kilogram per day. The first pair, six times twenty over ten, also gives twelve. V max takes the units of the dose rate, so here it is per kilogram. She said, I wrote this twice because you should get the same answer regardless of which way you use it.

card.m: V<sub>max</sub> = {{frac:R (K<sub>M</sub> + C<sub>ss</sub>)|C<sub>ss</sub>}}
V<sub>max</sub> in the units of R: mg/kg/day

segs.text: Reading the results back shows why a dose change matters so much. At ten milligrams per liter the level equals K M, so the elimination rate is half of V max: six, the dose rate she gave. At twenty, the rate is eight, two thirds of V max. So the closer the daily dose comes to V max, the larger the rise in level for each added milligram, and objective four uses K M and V max, not a simple proportion, to choose a new dose.

card.m: C<sub>ss</sub> = 10 mg/L = K<sub>M</sub>: R = {{frac:12 × 10|10 + 10}} = 6 = ½ V<sub>max</sub>
C<sub>ss</sub> = 20 mg/L: R = {{frac:12 × 20|10 + 20}} = 8 = ⅔ V<sub>max</sub>

segs.text: The usual errors come from the same lines. K M is a concentration, so a rate unit on K M is wrong. A level called low relative to V max is wrong in any option, because V max is a rate, read on the rate axis, and a level is compared only with K M, on the concentration axis. Subtracting the ratios in the wrong order makes K M negative. In the V max line, one pair's dose rate goes with that same pair's level, never with the other pair's level. The seventy two kilograms are used only when a dose for this patient is asked, in objective four.

card.m: K<sub>M</sub> in mg/L, never a rate unit
✗ low relative to V<sub>max</sub>: a rate, not a level
(R<sub>1</sub>/C<sub>1</sub>) − (R<sub>2</sub>/C<sub>2</sub>), in that order
V<sub>max</sub>: R and C<sub>ss</sub> from the same pair
